# Summary on Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish computer engineer and inventor, born into a family of intellectuals and mountaineers. After surviving serious injuries and active resistance during World War II, he pursued an engineering education and embarked on a remarkable career in computer design, beginning with early projects such as the AAH (Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics) and the AKAT-1, the world’s first transistor-based differential equations analyzer. In 1968, Karpiński completed the KAR-65 computer, which was the fastest Polish computer of its time but faced censorship and suppression, limiting its recognition and proliferation.
Karpiński's major achievement was the design of the K-202 minicomputer, started in 1970. It was an innovative, modular, asynchronous machine using Intel 4004 microchips that outperformed international competitors like the PDP-11. Despite its technical excellence and initial moderate political support, the project was stifled by political opposition, allegations of mismanagement, and lack of industrial backing. Only about 30 prototypes were produced, and the project was effectively shelved and renamed "Mera 400." Karpiński blamed sabotage and administrative incompetence for the failure, though critics point to his personal traits and the USSR-aligned technological priorities of the communist regime as contributing factors.
After the collapse of K-202’s prospects, Karpiński moved away from computer engineering, engaging in rural animal husbandry and later working in Switzerland on audio technology. In the 1990s, he attempted to commercialize inventions such as a hand-held text scanner and cash registers, though these ventures failed. Recognized posthumously with high state honors in Poland, his legacy remains controversial due to both his technological contributions and revealed past as a secret informant for Polish security services, providing technologically valuable intelligence, particularly during his travels abroad in the 1960s and 1970s.
